summary:
ARMSTRONG PROTOCOL is an interactive 2D lunar survival simulator developed for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take command of a Moon base and must keep their crew alive throughout a seven-day mission.

Through interconnected STEM-based minigames, students manage electrical power, produce oxygen, grow food, transport supplies, analyze solar radiation, and prepare for dangerous space weather events. Every decision involves trade-offs: using energy to produce oxygen may leave less power for food production or communications.

Built with Godot and GDScript, the game combines scientific concepts with resource management, problem-solving, and strategic decision-making.

Our goal is to make space engineering accessible, engaging, and educational. Instead of simply memorizing scientific facts, young learners experience how engineering systems depend on one another and discover how their choices affect mission survival and success.
details:
How it works

ARMSTRONG PROTOCOL is a 2D educational simulation in which the player operates an interconnected lunar outpost during a seven-day survival mission. The objective is to protect the crew, maintain essential resources, complete scientific operations, survive a solar storm, and transmit the mission report to Earth.

The game includes eight specialized modules:

  • GENESIS: Electrical power distribution and mission control.
  • VULCAN: Electrical engineering and circuit calculations.
  • ATLAS: Oxygen production through water electrolysis.
  • EDEN: Hydroponic food cultivation and resource management.
  • ORION: Cargo logistics and supply prioritization.
  • NYX: Solar radiation monitoring and risk assessment.
  • CONCORDIA: Radiation shielding and emergency shelter preparation.
  • HORIZON: Communication system configuration and mission reporting.

Educational impact

Unlike isolated educational quizzes, the game's systems share resources and create meaningful consequences. Players must decide how to allocate limited energy, water, oxygen, food, and supplies. A decision that benefits one system can create problems elsewhere.

The experience introduces concepts from chemistry, physics, biology, mathematics, engineering, and systems thinking through interactive challenges.

Technology and development

The project was developed using Godot Engine 4, GDScript, and 2D game design. It combines player movement, interactive terminals, resource management, mission progression, simulated engineering calculations, and event-driven challenges.

The team used AI-assisted development tools for parts of its programming and images generation.

Scientific foundations

The simulation draws on NASA educational and technical resources about environmental control and life support, oxygen generation, water recycling, radiation hazards, and lunar infrastructure.

Engineering parameters are simplified for educational gameplay. The game is not intended to reproduce exact spacecraft operating conditions.

Intended impact

Our goal is to help young learners understand that successful space exploration requires more than individual scientific knowledge. It requires cooperation between systems, careful planning, experimentation, and the ability to make decisions under constraints.
